summary: How to draw a system, find and rate its risks, change it while it is in use, get decisions accepted, design the teams, and what to read next.

blocks.title: C4 levels of zoom
rows: Your system as one box, its users and neighbors

items.text: Draw level 2 for a kata or an interview. In a real project, draw level 1 first.
Give each box a name and a job: "Orders (takes and tracks orders)", not "Service A".
Give each arrow a verb label and a direction from the part that starts the action.
Use a solid line for a call that waits. Use a dashed line for a message.
Show where data lives and who owns it. Make external systems look different.
Use one level of zoom in one diagram.
Use a sequence diagram for a hard flow, such as a payment timeout.
In a kata, attach each arrow to two shapes, so the connection is real.
Before you draw, write down who reads the diagram and what question it answers.
Sketch first. Make a clean version only when the design is stable.

items.when: You must replace an old system
items.use: Small reversible steps, not one rewrite

items.when: You replace an old system function by function
You replace one part that other code calls
You must trust the new results before you switch
A structure changes and its users must move
The new path must start with a few users
An architecture rule must not decay
items.use: A fitness function, run with the tests

items.when: You must find the debt that costs most
items.use: Change frequency combined with change difficulty

items.text: Rate each risk as impact times likelihood, each from 1 to 3. A score of 6 to 9 is high.
In risk storming, each person rates the risks alone first. Then the group discusses the disagreements.
A mitigation moves risk. A new cache lowers a scalability risk and adds an availability risk.
"Accept" is a valid response. Record it with a name and a date in a decision record.
In a strangler fig, the hard part is the data. Each piece needs one owner while both run.
A rule that is only in a document is broken in months. A rule that fails the build stays.
Pay back debt in the parts that change often. Debt in untouched code costs nothing.
"The architecture is bad" gets no budget. Connect the change to a business result.
Count a migration as done only when the old part is gone. Budget for its removal.
Avoid dual writes. Give each piece of data one owner, and copy it through events.
Conway's law: organizations build systems that copy their own communication structure.
Parts owned by different teams need clear, stable interfaces.
To get independent services, create teams that each own one service from start to production.
Explain the same decision in a different way to each person. It is translation, not dishonesty.
Bring two or three options, with the trade-offs, and a recommendation.
Use numbers: "four seconds for the order page", not "too slow".
Disagree, and then commit. Say your concern clearly once.
Give developers the reason, not only the rule.
Demonstration defeats discussion. Build a small test of both options, and measure the result.
Ask each person for an opinion directly, not "any objections?".

items.when: You start, and want the base of this app
You want to know how databases and replication really work
You split services and data, with sagas
You want to know how systems fail in production
You need bounded contexts and a shared business language
You need service levels, error budgets, and alerts
You want team structure and architecture to fit
You prepare for the classic interview questions
You need evidence that links delivery practice to business results
You want modules that hide complexity

blocks.title: Select a team type and interaction mode

items.when: A team delivers value for one stream of work
A part needs rare, deep specialist knowledge
Several teams repeat deployment and monitoring work
items.use: A platform team, run as a product

items.when: Teams must learn a new skill or practice
items.use: An enabling team that then steps back

items.when: Two teams discover a new boundary or technology
A capability is stable and well understood
One team helps another learn or remove obstacles

items.text: Reverse Conway maneuver: change the team structure first, to get the architecture you want.
The maneuver fails if the new teams still share one database and one release.
Most teams must be stream-aligned. The other three types exist to reduce their load.
Keep a team long-lived and small: up to about 7 to 9 people.
Limit the responsibilities of a team to what fits its cognitive load.
Give each domain to one team. A team with a complex domain owns no other domain.
Each service adds deployment, monitoring, and on-call load. Twenty small services can cost more than one.
Time-box collaboration. Move to X-as-a-Service when the boundary is clear.
Start with the thinnest viable platform. It can be a wiki page or a set of templates.
Use the business domain as the default fracture plane.
